hints: Start by reminding yourself what volatility really means, how easily a liquid turns into a gas by breaking forces between molecules.
Notice both exist as simple diatomic molecules, $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$, so compare their electrons and how easily their electron clouds can be distorted.
Connect stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces to harder evaporation, then pick the element that escapes more easily for the right reason.
walkthrough:
**What volatility tells us**

Think of volatility as how keen a liquid is to escape into the gas phase. A more volatile liquid has weaker forces between its molecules, so less energy is needed to separate them.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{weaker intermolecular forces} \rightarrow \text{more volatile (lower boiling point)}$$

**Identify the forces involved**

Both chlorine and bromine are non-polar diatomic molecules, $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$. The only forces between their molecules are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces.

**Compare chlorine and bromine**

Bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms, with many more electrons (35 per Br atom versus 17 per Cl atom). More electrons means a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so temporary dipoles form more easily and the London forces are stronger in bromine.

Trend:
$$\text{strength of London forces: } \text{Br}_2 > \text{Cl}_2$$

**Link strength to volatility**

Because $\text{Br}_2$ has stronger intermolecular forces, it holds its molecules together more tightly and is less volatile. That is why bromine is a liquid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas. So chlorine is the more volatile element because the forces are greater in bromine.

options.A: Incorrect. The explanation part is right that forces are greater in bromine, but the identity is backwards. Stronger forces mean molecules are held more tightly, so bromine is less volatile, not more volatile.
options.B: Incorrect on both parts. Bromine is not more volatile than chlorine, and forces are not greater in chlorine. This reverses the effect of more electrons and greater polarisability in bromine.
options.C: Correct. Chlorine is more volatile because its London forces are weaker. Bromine has more electrons and is more polarisable, so its instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are stronger and it evaporates less readily.
options.D: Half right but half wrong. Chlorine is indeed the more volatile element, but the reason given is reversed. Forces are greater in bromine, not in chlorine, due to bromine's larger electron cloud.
